newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cuprus police say Turk confessed to espionage.
newsitem.headline: Cuprus police say Turk confessed to espionage.

text.p: Police in Cyprus said on Tuesday a Turk living in the south of the divided island had confessed to spying on Greek Cypriot military positions over the past 18 months for Turkey.

The suspect, identified as Nejip Sari Cicekli, 45, from Turkey, is being held on suspicion of spying on security and military positions. Two Turkish Cypriots detained with him are suspected accomplices, police spokesman Glafcos Xenos told Reuters.
"We are examining an espionage case and this man has confessed to many things," Xenos said. He said Cicekli admitted spying on military sites for Turkey.
Police said they found military documents, videos with military information and maps of Greek Cypriot army camps in Cicekli's car and home in the southern coastal town of Limassol.
"We are studying all the documents found...it is going to be a considerable task," said Xenos, adding that most documents were in Turkish.

All three men were living in Limassol in south Cyprus, the mainly Greek Cypriot part of the island under the control of the internationally recognised Greek Cypriot-led government. Cicekli has lived in the south since 1982, after leaving the northern Turkish area.
Greek and Turkish Cypriots have lived separately since 1974, when Turkish troops invaded northern Cyprus in response to a Greek Cypriot coup backed by the military junta then ruling Athens.
Negotiations to unite the two communities in a bicommunal federation have stalled.

Turkey has some 30,000 troops in northern Cyprus, declared a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in 1983 but recognised only by Ankara. The 10,000 strong Greek Cypriot national guard is engaged in a comrehensive programme to upgrade its capabilities.
In January the Greek Cypriots agreed to buy surface-to-air missiles from Russia. Turkey has threatened a military strike if deployment of the missiles next year goes ahead.
